IR Curve Generation Config Process Parameter Value Table
One named process-parameter value of an ir_curve_generation_config,
referencing its yield_curve_process_parameter_definition. This is the
"value" half of the row-based parameter architecture: an IR curve
generation config stores its process parameters as one row per
definition supplies the vocabulary (name, description, bounds), and
the mapping layer materialises these rows into the strongly-typed
The (config_id, parameter_definition_id) pair is unique: each
parameter appears at most once per config. A hand-written DB trigger
(not the codegen single-argument Validations mechanism, which cannot
express a two-column lookup) enforces that the definition's
process_type_code matches the config's process_type -- a config
driven by TWO_FACTOR_GAUSSIAN may only carry values whose definitions
belong to TWO_FACTOR_GAUSSIAN. Both soft FKs are additionally
validated at insert time by the generated validation functions. No
standalone UI: value rows are edited from inside the IR curve
generation config detail dialog, which reads definitions and value
rows via the normal codegen repositories.

A generic, self-referencing hierarchy node. The Market Simulator tree is
drawn directly from these rows rather than parsed out of a feed's
source_name string: one root folder per party ("Synthetic"), with
"FX"), and instrument-type folders (e.g. "FX Rates") nested beneath it.
fx_spot_generation_config rows reference their immediate parent folder
via folder_id. kind distinguishes what a given row represents; =
collection_id= is populated only for kind 'collection'= rows, linking
back to the market_data_generation_config it represents (that entity
remains the source of truth for name/description/enabled/dataset_id;
this row's own name is kept in sync for uniform hierarchy display).
Having real, queryable folder rows (rather than string-parsing) lets any
the shell, or a future UI

of each reimplementing the tree-walk itself.

One FX fixing that an fx_spot_generation_config whose price_source is
fixing may start from. A feed reads its items in rank order and starts from the
first that has a fixing: the latest on or before the date of the market clock, or
on a stated date. The window sets how many days of fixings measure the
volatility. An item may quote the pair the other way round, and the feed then reads
it as one over the value. Party- and tenant-scoped.

A typed sub-configuration owned by a market_data_generation_config. Describes
how to synthesise the tick stream for a single FX spot rate: which ORE market
key it produces, the starting price, the tick cadence, and the price process.
The price process is a Gaussian Mixture Model whose components are held
separately as gmm_component rows. Scoped to a tenant and a party.

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
One row of the raw instrument grid (the "Curve Template") an
ir_curve_generation_config publishes: which tenor period, priced as
swap-equivalent -- see ores.refdata.instrument_code), in what order.
Every entry is modelled as a genuine [start, end) period rather than
a single maturity label: start_tenor_code/end_tenor_code are both
ordinary tenor references resolved through the same
zero-duration PERIOD/DAY tenor already in the catalog, resolving
directly to the horizon's spot date -- not a null/sentinel hack);
interval instruments (FRAs) set it to the period's own front tenor
(e.g. '3M' for a 3x6 FRA whose end_tenor_code is '6M'). This
symmetric shape is what lets the tenor-collision validator
period overlaps via plain windows_overlap(), without a special case
for point vs. interval instruments. Entries belong to a parent config
via ir_curve_config_id, the same one-config-many-children shape
fx_spot_generation_config's gmm_component rows use. Every entry's
published rate is derived from the parent config's short-rate
process's discount_factor() at the tenor's maturity -- never an
independently-noised value -- so the published tick batch is, by
construction, a slice of one internally consistent curve. Party- and

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
A catalogue of the providers whose market data the synthetic feeds simulate.
A system-scope collection names the provider it stands for, so the installation
can run a simulated Bloomberg, LSEG or CME once and every tenant reads it
as that provider's data. Every collection names its provider, so every feed has
one. A reference set such as the ORE examples is a provider of its own.
Every provider here is simulated, and the synthetic screens show it without a
mark, because everything on them is synthetic. Every source name a provider's feed
publishes on starts synthetic.<provider code>., so a simulated feed is never read
as the real one. A real provider integration, when one comes, belongs in market data
Scoped to ores.synthetic (not ores.refdata) because only synthetic
generation uses it today, following the yield_curve_process_type
precedent. Managed by the system tenant.

Yield Curve Process Parameter Definition Table
Reference data table describing, per yield_curve_process_type, the
named parameters that process accepts and their validation bounds. This
is the "vocabulary" half of the row-based parameter architecture: an
ir_curve_generation_config stores its process parameters as
definition, and the mapping layer materialises those rows into the
parameter; four fields drive the parameter table: display_name
(the English name), symbol (the Greek letter, where one is
conventional), short_label (the layperson name shown in Simple
mode) and description (the rich tooltip text). min_value/
max_value (NULL = unbounded) plus default_value drive the
Why this exists as a table rather than hardcoded structs: it makes the
parameter vocabulary queryable and extensible -- adding a new model or
parameter is a seed-data change, not a schema or code change, and the
same vocabulary drives the DB (validation of value rows), the mapping
layer (expected parameter names), and the UI (rows to display). Managed
by the system tenant as read-only reference data; tenant users never
edit definitions, only the values of their own configs.

One book a trade generation config books into. The book scope of a
configuration is a set, so it is a repeating field set and lives here, one
row per book, rather than a column on the config: a party holds up to twenty
books and the population spreads across them.
The row references a real book of the config's own party. The trade booking
trigger refuses a book that belongs to another party, so a row naming one
would write no trade. The generator resolves the reference rather than
inventing it, and that resolution is what fails loudly when the reference is
Book-scope rows belong to a parent config through config_id, the same
one-config-many-children shape gmm_component uses for its parent

A named recipe for the trades one party's books receive. It is the
population as configuration: a reviewer reads the row and the two scope
The row names the booking party, the instrument family, the tenor and
notional bands, the as-of anchor and the seed. The book scope and the
counterparty scope are the two multi-valued field sets and live in child
tables, one row per book and one row per counterparty, the same
one-config-many-children shape fx_spot_generation_config uses for its
gmm_component rows and ir_curve_generation_config for its
The booking party is the row's own party_id. The writer sets
app.current_party_id to it before each trade, because the trading
insert triggers overwrite the instrument's party from session state.
The two scope lists are the child tables trade_generation_book and
trade_generation_counterparty, one row per book and one row per
counterparty. Both are edited from this configuration's detail dialog.
The population is a function of the pair (seed, as-of anchor). The seed
pins the shape of the population and not the identity of its rows. The
same pair emits the same rows; a later anchor moves the population
forward rather than repeating it. See
with a trade population]], "What makes a seed deterministic".

To modify, update the template and regenerate.
One fixing date of a variance_calibration_input: the fixing as it was stored, the
number read from it, and the daily log return it gives in the pair's market
convention. A point the fit may not use is kept with the reason, such as a value
that is not a number, so the input states every date the window held and not only
log_return is the return from the previous used point to this one, after the
inversion the input names. The first used point has no return, and a point whose
value cannot be read has neither a value nor a return.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
One capture of the data a variance calibration reads: the item that was read for a
pair, under which calibration policy, over which window, and whether its value was
inverted to reach the pair's market convention. Each fixing date of the window is
a variance_calibration_input_point, kept whether it was used or not, so a reader
can see every number a fit saw. A fit reads only a stored input, never the live
fixings, so the same input always gives the same fit. See "A calibration is stored
and reviewed before a feed runs it" in
Who captured the input and when are the performed_by and valid_from every row
carries. A capture over the same window of the same item is a new version of the
input, not a second input, by the natural key: the party, the fixing URI and the
window. The item names the pair it is read for, so the pair is not part of the key.
AUTO-GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY
To modify, update the template and regenerate.
One GJR-GARCH shape of a pair's daily variance and the evidence a reviewer judges
it by. A fitted calibration names the variance_calibration_input it was fitted
from and the version of the method that fitted it; an authored one names no input
and is reviewed like any other. A feed runs only a calibration that is approved,
and names it. See "A calibration is stored and reviewed before a feed runs it" in
A calibration is proposed when it is stored. A person approves or rejects it and
states why in state_reason; approving one makes the pair's earlier approval
superseded in the same change, so one approved calibration of a pair is current.
Each decision is a new version of the row, so its history shows who decided what
and when. A fit that could not be made, for too few returns or a shape at the
stationarity bound, is stored as rejected with the reason, so the attempt is kept;
such a row may have no shape, so the shape is required, and admissible, in the
other three states only. Each bound is written so that a missing value or NaN
fails it: a check passes on null, and PostgreSQL orders NaN above every number. A
value that is present is finite in every state, rejected included, so the audit
trail holds no NaN. The evidence of a fit agrees with its method: an authored shape
has no starts, returns or likelihood, and a fit that was not rejected has all three.
The checks do not tie persistence to the three parameters, because p_minus is
not stored; the fit that writes a calibration owns that equality.
persistence is alpha + gamma p_minus + beta, with p_minus the share of the
daily return's variance that falls on negative days, so it is stored rather than
recomputed from the three parameters alone.

Reference data table enumerating the i_yield_curve_process engines
can construct: VASICEK, COX_INGERSOLL_ROSS, HULL_WHITE. Replaces an inline
catalogue row per engine -- same reasoning as promoting
instrument_code from a hardcoded list to a real reference-data table.
i_yield_curve_process engine selection is specific to synthetic IR curve
generation, its only consumer today; not promoted to shared refdata
until it is genuinely shared by something else, per this story's own
payment_frequency precedent. Managed by the system tenant.
